title: Engineering organic–inorganic–polymer hybrid electrolytes for transition bimetallic sulfides@MXene nanocomposites toward advanced energy storage and electrochemical sensing
content: Next-generation wearable and self-powered diagnostic systems have attracted great interest in the development of multifunctional electrode materials that can be used simultaneously for energy storage and electrochemical sensing applications. This paper reports the synthesis and physicochemical evaluation of a MXene-doped vanadium–niobium sulfide (VNbS@MXene) composite, along with a systematic evaluation of its electrochemical behavior in four different electrolyte systems, and the demonstration of dual functionality for energy storage and glucose sensing applications. The synergistic combination of high-conductivity nanosheets provides plenty of redox-active sites and high electron transport pathways, which allow the improvement of electrochemical kinetics. Electrochemical characteristics of the electrode were tested in four types of electrolyte systems, and the hybrid electrolyte design demonstrated the most desirable electrochemical characteristics, as it showed better ionic conductivity and stronger ion-electrode interactions. Under optimized conditions, the VNbS@MXene electrode achieved a high specific charge storage capacity of 1296.26 C g−1. The VNbS@MXene//AC hybrid system presented the highest specific capacity of 291 C g−1 and an energy density of 64.71 Wh kg−1 and a power density of 1840 W kg−1, indicating its ability to bridge batteries and supercapacitors. Besides energy storage performance, the VNbS@MXene electrode had excellent electrocatalytic activity in non-enzymatic glucose sensing with a sensitivity of 19.8 µA mM−1 cm−2, a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.015 mM, a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 0.05 mM, and a response time of 3.45 s. The sensor was shown to be highly selective, repeatable, and reproducible, while recovery experiments in simulated plasma and pooled human serum verified its suitability for glucose sensing in complex biological matrices. The combination of high-energy storage and sensitive glucose detection reveals the versatility of the VNbS@MXene composite and turns out to be useful in self-powered sensing systems and wearable diagnostic tools of the future.
